name: Object-Oriented Programming
description: Encapsulation, polymorphism, SOLID, composition over inheritance and the failure modes of each.

modules.name: The Big Picture
modules.description: What Object-Oriented Programming is, what it is for, and the words everything else builds on.

cards.prompt: What is object-oriented programming (OOP)?
cards.answer: A style of programming that organises code around objects — bundles of data (fields) together with the functions that operate on that data (methods) — instead of keeping data and functions separate.
cards.explanation: An object models a thing in the problem: a `BankAccount` holds a balance and offers `deposit` and `withdraw`. OOP became the dominant style in the 1990s through C++ and Java and remains central to Java, C#, Python, Kotlin and Swift.

cards.prompt: Class vs object
cards.answer: A class is a blueprint describing what data and behaviour its objects have; an object (instance) is one concrete thing built from that blueprint.

right.title: Object (instance)
points: Created many times at run time

cards.explanation: Two `Dog` objects share the same methods but each has its own `name`. Creating an object from a class is called instantiation.

cards.prompt: What are fields (attributes) and methods?
cards.answer: Fields are the data an object holds (a `Dog`'s `name` and `age`); methods are the functions defined on the class that act on that data (`bark()`, `birthday()`).
cards.explanation: Inside a method, the object itself is available as `self` (Python) or `this` (Java, C#, JavaScript, C++, Kotlin), so the method can read and change that particular object's fields.

cards.prompt: What is a constructor?
cards.answer: A special method that runs when an object is created, to set up its initial state — `__init__` in Python, a method named after the class in Java and C#, `constructor` in JavaScript.
cards.explanation: Constructors are the place to require the data an object cannot be valid without, so that no half-initialised object can ever exist.

cards.prompt: What is an interface?
cards.answer: A contract that lists methods a type promises to provide, without saying how. Any class implementing the interface can be used wherever the interface is expected.
cards.explanation: Interfaces let code depend on capabilities ("something that can `save()`") rather than on specific classes, which makes swapping implementations and testing much easier. Java, C#, Go, TypeScript and Kotlin all have them; Python uses protocols and abstract base classes.

cards.prompt: Which mainstream languages are object-oriented, and which are not?
cards.answer: Strongly OOP: Java, C#, Kotlin, Swift, Ruby. Multi-paradigm with full OOP support: Python, C++, JavaScript/TypeScript, PHP. Not class-based: C (procedural), Go (structs and interfaces, no classes or inheritance), Rust (structs and traits), Haskell (functional).
cards.explanation: OOP is a tool, not a requirement: Go and Rust deliberately dropped inheritance and still model problems well with composition and interfaces/traits.

modules.name: Pillars & Principles
modules.description: The four pillars, SOLID, and what each principle is actually protecting you from.

cards.prompt: Name the four pillars of OOP and what each buys you.
cards.answer: Encapsulation (hide state behind an interface so invariants hold), abstraction (expose the what, not the how), inheritance (reuse and specialise a type), polymorphism (one interface, many implementations).
cards.explanation: Encapsulation is the load-bearing one: if callers can put an object into an invalid state, none of the others save you. Inheritance is the most abused — it couples subclasses to the base's implementation forever.

cards.prompt: What does SOLID stand for?
cards.answer: Single responsibility, Open/closed, Liskov substitution, Interface segregation, Dependency inversion.
cards.explanation: They are heuristics against specific pains: SRP against change ripple, OCP against modifying tested code, LSP against broken polymorphism, ISP against fat interfaces forcing empty implementations, DIP against high-level policy depending on low-level detail.

cards.prompt: Why is this the textbook Liskov violation?
cards.answer: Code written against Rectangle assumes setting width leaves height alone. Square breaks that assumption, so a Square is not substitutable for a Rectangle even though 'a square is a rectangle' is true in geometry.
cards.explanation: LSP is about behavioural contracts, not taxonomy. Subtypes may weaken preconditions and strengthen postconditions, never the reverse. The fix here is composition or immutable shapes — mutability is what creates the contract in the first place.

cards.prompt: Composition vs inheritance
cards.answer: Inheritance is a compile-time 'is-a' that inherits implementation; composition is a runtime 'has-a' that delegates behaviour.

left.title: Inheritance
points: Fragile base class: base changes break subclasses
Deep hierarchies get impossible to reason about

right.title: Composition
points: Explicit delegation — more typing, more clarity

cards.explanation: 'Favour composition over inheritance' exists because inheritance couples you to a base class's implementation details permanently. Use inheritance for genuine subtyping with a stable contract; use composition — or interfaces plus delegation — for reuse.

cards.prompt: Your business logic imports a concrete Postgres client. Why is that a problem, and what does dependency inversion do about it?
cards.answer: High-level policy now depends on a low-level detail — you cannot test it without a database, or change stores without editing the logic. Invert it: the domain declares a repository interface, and the Postgres adapter implements it.
cards.explanation: The interface belongs with the consumer, not the implementation — that is the actual inversion. This is the core of hexagonal/ports-and-adapters and clean architecture: dependencies point inward, toward policy.

cards.prompt: What is wrong with this getter?
cards.answer: It returns the internal mutable list, so any caller can add or clear items behind the class's back — every invariant Order maintains is now unenforceable. Return an unmodifiable view or a copy.
cards.explanation: Encapsulation is about controlling *mutation*, not about writing getters. `Collections.unmodifiableList(items)`, `List.copyOf(items)` or exposing intent-revealing methods (`addItem`, `total()`) all restore the boundary.

modules.name: Mechanics & Alternatives
modules.description: Dispatch, abstract types, interfaces and where OOP gives way to other models.

cards.prompt: Static vs dynamic dispatch
cards.answer: Static dispatch resolves the target at compile time; dynamic dispatch resolves at runtime through a vtable or method table.

right.title: Dynamic
points: Resolved by the object's runtime type

cards.explanation: Overloading is static (chosen by declared argument types); overriding is dynamic (chosen by runtime type). Mixing them up produces the classic surprise where an overload is selected on the base type you declared, not the object you passed.

cards.prompt: Abstract class vs interface
cards.answer: An abstract class can hold state and partial implementation, but a class can extend only one; an interface is a contract, and a class can implement many.

left.title: Abstract class
points: Versioning: adding a method is safe

cards.explanation: Rule of thumb: interfaces express *what a thing can do* and should be small; abstract classes express *what a family of things shares*. If you find yourself faking multiple inheritance with abstract classes, you wanted composition.

resources.title: Microsoft Learn — Abstract and sealed classes

cards.prompt: The Law of Demeter is often summarised as "only talk to your immediate ___" — avoid chains like `order.getCustomer().getAddress().getCity()`.
cards.answer: friends
cards.explanation: Every link in a train wreck is a dependency you did not declare and cannot refactor around. Ask the collaborator to do the work (`order.shippingCity()`) rather than reaching through it. Fluent builders and stream pipelines are the deliberate exception — they return objects of the same abstraction.

cards.prompt: What is an anaemic domain model, and why is it considered an anti-pattern?
cards.answer: Domain objects that are pure data bags with getters and setters, while all behaviour lives in separate 'service' classes. It is OO in syntax only — the data and the rules that govern it are separated, so invariants cannot be enforced.
cards.explanation: The practical symptom is validation logic duplicated across services and objects that can be constructed in invalid states. The counter-argument: in simple CRUD systems the extra ceremony buys nothing. Judge by how many rules actually govern the data.

cards.prompt: When does a functional style beat an object-oriented one, and vice versa?
cards.answer: Functional wins for data transformation pipelines, concurrency and anything where immutability removes whole bug classes. OO wins where you have long-lived entities with identity, state transitions and invariants to protect.
cards.explanation: The expression problem frames it: OO makes adding new *types* easy and new *operations* hard; FP makes adding operations easy and types hard. Most modern codebases mix both — immutable values and pure transforms inside, objects at the boundaries.

modules.name: Design Principles in Practice
modules.description: Cohesion and coupling, SOLID in detail, DRY, tell-don't-ask, value objects and invariants.

cards.prompt: Cohesion vs coupling
cards.answer: Cohesion is how strongly the parts inside a module belong together; coupling is how much a module depends on others. Aim for high cohesion and low coupling.

left.title: Cohesion (inside)
points: Things that change together live together
Raise it by splitting by responsibility

right.title: Coupling (between)
points: How much A must know about B
High: shared globals, reaching into internals
Lower it with interfaces and events

cards.explanation: Nearly every design principle is a special case of this pair. A change that ripples across many modules signals high coupling; a class whose methods share no fields signals low cohesion and wants splitting. Measure design by how many places a typical change touches.

cards.prompt: An `Invoice` class calculates totals, renders a PDF and saves itself to the database. What does the single responsibility principle say, and how do you split it?
cards.answer: A class should have one reason to change — here three: pricing rules, document layout and persistence, each owned by a different person or team. Keep `Invoice` for the domain calculations, and move rendering to an `InvoicePdfRenderer` and storage to an `InvoiceRepository`.
cards.explanation: SRP is about axes of change, not about a class doing "one thing" in the tiniest sense. Over-applying it produces dozens of one-method classes that are harder to follow. Split when two responsibilities actually change for different reasons.

resources.title: Robert C. Martin — The Single Responsibility Principle

cards.prompt: What principle does this violate, and what is the symptom?
cards.answer: Interface segregation: `ReadOnlyReport` is forced to implement write methods it cannot support, so it throws. Split the fat interface into role interfaces — `Readable`, `Writable` — and let classes implement only what they can honour.
cards.explanation: Throwing `UnsupportedOperationException` from an interface method is the tell. It also breaks Liskov substitution, since callers of `Storage.save` cannot trust it. Small interfaces defined by what the *client* needs are easier to implement, mock and evolve.

cards.prompt: What does the open/closed principle mean in practice?
cards.answer: Code should be open for extension but closed for modification: add new behaviour by adding new code (a new strategy, handler or subclass) rather than editing tested code — typically by depending on an abstraction the new code can implement.
cards.explanation: The practical form is "don't make every new case an edit to the same switch statement". Apply it at the points that actually vary; making everything extensible up front is speculative generality. The first time a switch gains its third case is a good moment.

cards.prompt: Two functions look identical today. Should you merge them?
cards.answer: Only if they represent the same knowledge — the same business rule that must change together. DRY is about not duplicating knowledge, not about deduplicating similar-looking code. Coincidental similarity merged into one function becomes a tangle of flags once the two uses diverge.
cards.explanation: The rule of three is a useful brake: tolerate duplication until the third occurrence reveals what actually varies. "Duplication is far cheaper than the wrong abstraction" — undoing a bad shared helper is harder than extracting a good one later.

cards.prompt: What design smell is this, and how do you fix it?
cards.answer: "Ask" style: the caller pulls data out of `account` and makes the decision itself, so the rule lives outside the object that owns the data — and gets duplicated wherever withdrawals happen. Tell the object what to do: `account.withdraw(amount)`, which enforces the rule internally.
cards.explanation: Tell-don't-ask keeps behaviour next to the data it governs, so invariants are enforced in one place. Getters are not evil, but a caller that reads several fields to decide something is usually doing the object's job.

cards.prompt: What is a value object, and why use one instead of primitives?
cards.answer: An immutable object defined entirely by its values, with no identity — `Money(10, "GBP")`, `EmailAddress`, `DateRange`. Two with equal values are interchangeable. It validates itself on construction, so an invalid one cannot exist.
cards.explanation: Replacing primitives (primitive obsession) with value objects moves validation to one place and makes signatures self-documenting: `transfer(Money, AccountId)` cannot be called with arguments swapped the way `transfer(double, String)` can. Records and data classes make them cheap to write.

cards.prompt: What is a class invariant, and where should it be enforced?
cards.answer: A condition that must hold for every valid instance at every public boundary — `start <= end`, `balance >= 0` for this account type, "an order has at least one line". Establish it in the constructor and preserve it in every mutating method; reject operations that would break it.
cards.explanation: If invalid objects can be constructed, every consumer must re-validate defensively. Factories and constructors that fail fast, plus immutability where possible, make invariants hold by construction rather than by convention.

modules.name: Polymorphism & Type Relationships
modules.description: Kinds of polymorphism, overloading versus overriding, multiple inheritance and mixins, identity versus equality.

cards.prompt: What are the three main kinds of polymorphism?
cards.answer: Subtype polymorphism — code works with a base type and runs the subclass's override (virtual methods, interfaces). Parametric polymorphism — code is generic over types (`List<T>`, generics). Ad-hoc polymorphism — the same name does different things per type (overloading, operator overloading, type classes and traits).
cards.explanation: OOP tends to mean only the first, but modern languages lean heavily on the second and third: Rust traits and Haskell type classes give ad-hoc polymorphism without inheritance; Go interfaces give subtype polymorphism structurally.

cards.prompt: What does this print?
cards.answer: Animal Dog
cards.explanation: `describe(a)` picks the overload at compile time from the declared type `Animal`, so it prints "Animal" even though the object is a Dog. `a.name()` is an override, chosen at runtime from the actual object, so it prints "Dog". Overloading is static; overriding is dynamic.

resources.title: Java Tutorials — Overriding and hiding methods

cards.prompt: What is the diamond problem, and how do different languages handle it?
cards.answer: When a class inherits from two classes that share a base, which version of an inherited method or field wins, and is the base duplicated? C++ requires `virtual` inheritance to share the base; Python linearises with C3 MRO; Java and C# allow multiple inheritance only of interfaces (default-method conflicts must be resolved explicitly).
cards.explanation: Mixins and traits are the pragmatic middle ground: small bundles of behaviour composed into a class without an "is-a" claim. Most designs never need multiple implementation inheritance — composition covers it more clearly.

resources.title: Wikipedia — Multiple inheritance — the diamond problem

cards.prompt: Identity vs equality
cards.answer: Identity asks "are these the same object?" (same reference); equality asks "do these represent the same value?" (as defined by `equals`/`__eq__`).

left.title: Identity
points: Entities: a stable ID across changes

cards.explanation: Entities (a customer, an order) have identity that persists as their attributes change — compare them by ID. Value objects (money, dates) have no identity — compare them by value. Mixing the two up leads to duplicate rows or objects that vanish from hash sets.
